question: Multilingualism is one of the building blocks of the EU and a European ideal that the founding fathers hold dear. However, the findings of the Lequesne report are alarming: they reveal that the use of French is in decline, giving way to the hegemony of English. Between 1999 and 2019, the number of Commission documents with French as the source language fell from 34 % to 3.7 %.

In 2019, the Commission issued 85 % of its documents in English. However, there is an obvious democratic problem with making English – the official language of only 1 % of EU citizens – the main working language. Only using English also helps to spread the influence of the US across our institutions. Is the European Commission aware that this trend towards monolingualism threatens its independence and democracy?
answer: As the Commission noted in its replies to E-4480/19 and to E-6874/20 and in the replies referred to therei n (1), the rules governing the languages of the institutions of the European Union are determined by the Counci l (2), and the Commission has no competence in the matter.

Those rules are laid down in Regulation 1/1958 (3), according to which the EU institutions currently have 24 official and working languages, including English. The Commission promotes multilingualism as a guiding principle for fair use of the official languages of the EU, and it continues to use all 24 EU official and working languages in its activities.

Within the Commission, everyone is free to express themselves, orally or in writing, in a language of their choice, allowing them to communicate effectively with their colleagues. The use of any language by and within the Commission does not threaten its independence, nor does it have an impact on European democracy.
P-003541/2020 and E-005329/2020. Article 342 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A31958R0001
